traditions.name: Second Temple Judaism
traditions.summary: The religion of the Judean and diaspora Jewish communities from the completion of the rebuilt Jerusalem Temple (c. 516 BCE) until its destruction by Rome in 70 CE. It centred on Temple sacrifice and priesthood alongside the Torah, and was internally diverse, including groups such as Pharisees, Sadducees and Essenes who differed over law, purity and authority.

sources.title: The Second Temple (Lawrence H. Schiffman, From Text to Tradition)
sources.publisher: Center for Online Judaic Studies / Ktav

traditions.name: Rabbinic Judaism
traditions.summary: The form of Judaism that became normative after the fall of the Second Temple, organised around the authority of the sages (rabbis) and their interpretation of the Written Torah together with the Oral Torah, which according to rabbinic tradition was also given at Sinai. Its foundational literature is the Mishnah (c. 200 CE) and the Talmuds, and it places Torah study, prayer and halakhah (Jewish law) at the centre of religious life.

traditions.name: Karaite Judaism
traditions.summary: A Jewish movement that recognises the Hebrew Bible (Tanakh) alone as authoritative for law and doctrine and rejects the rabbinic Oral Torah and Talmud as binding. Karaites interpret scripture directly, which produces distinctive practices and calendar reckoning; Karaites themselves regard their Judaism as the original form, while historians usually trace the movement to 8th-9th century Babylonia and Persia.

sources.title: Biblical Exegesis as a Source of Jewish Pluralism: The Case of the Karaites (Daniel J. Lasker)

traditions.name: Hasidic Judaism
traditions.summary: A religious revival movement that arose in Podolia in the second quarter of the 18th century around Israel ben Eliezer, the Ba'al Shem Tov (d. 1760), and spread across Eastern Europe. Drawing on Kabbalah, it emphasises devekut (attachment to God), joyful and fervent prayer and the spiritual leadership of the tzaddik or rebbe, and it later divided into many dynastic courts that continue today.

sources.title: Hasidism: Historical Overview
sources.publisher: YIVO Encyclopedia of Jews in Eastern Europe

traditions.name: Orthodox Judaism
traditions.summary: The collective name for traditionalist Jewish communities that hold the Written and Oral Torah to be divinely given and halakhah to be binding and essentially unchangeable. Orthodox Jews generally understand themselves as continuing rabbinic Judaism rather than founding a new movement; historians describe 'Orthodoxy' as a self-conscious stance and label that took shape in early-to-mid 19th-century Central Europe in response to Enlightenment and Reform. It ranges from Neo-Orthodox/Modern Orthodox currents (associated with Samson Raphael Hirsch) to Haredi communities.

sources.title: Responses to Reform Movement's Emergence: Orthodox and Conservative
Samson Raphael Hirsch: The Father of Neo-Orthodoxy
Jeffrey C. Blutinger on the history of the label 'Orthodox' (Modern Judaism)

traditions.name: Reform Judaism
traditions.summary: A modernising movement that began in early 19th-century Germany and holds that Jewish belief and practice can and should evolve with changing times. It introduced vernacular prayer and sermons, choirs and organ music, and confirmation, and in its classical form (e.g. the 1885 Pittsburgh Platform) regarded ritual law as non-binding while stressing Judaism's ethical teachings.

traditions.name: Conservative Judaism
traditions.summary: A movement (called Masorti outside North America) that upholds the authority of halakhah and traditional observance while holding that Jewish law has developed historically and may continue to change through scholarly and rabbinic process. It traces its ideas to Zacharias Frankel's 'positive-historical' Judaism and its institutional base to the Jewish Theological Seminary in New York; it is often characterised as standing between Orthodoxy and Reform.

sources.title: Conservative Judaism (Pamela S. Nadell, Encyclopedia of Religion)
Responses to Reform Movement's Emergence: Orthodox and Conservative

traditions.name: Early Christianity
traditions.summary: Early Christianity began as a movement within Second Temple Judaism centred on Jesus of Nazareth, whose followers proclaimed him the Messiah after his execution in Jerusalem around 30 CE. It spread through Jewish and Gentile communities across the Roman world and beyond, developing creeds, councils and episcopal structures. The end date of 1054 is a conventional modelling choice for the undivided church; both the Catholic and the Eastern Orthodox churches claim continuity with it.

traditions.name: Church of the East
traditions.summary: The Church of the East is the historic Syriac-speaking church of the Persian (Sasanian) Empire, centred on Seleucia-Ctesiphon, which once extended its missions to Central Asia, India and China. It did not accept the Council of Ephesus (431) and today is represented chiefly by the Assyrian Church of the East and the Ancient Church of the East. In the West it was long called 'Nestorian', a label the church itself regards as pejorative and which many scholars consider misleading.

traditions.name: Oriental Orthodoxy
traditions.summary: The Oriental Orthodox churches are the communion of churches that did not accept the Council of Chalcedon (451): the Coptic, Ethiopian, Eritrean, Syriac, Armenian and Malankara (Indian) Orthodox churches. They accept the first three ecumenical councils and hold a miaphysite Christology based on Cyril of Alexandria's formula of 'one incarnate nature of the Word'. The older label 'Monophysite' is now generally regarded as inaccurate, and official dialogue with the Eastern Orthodox since 1985 has produced Christological agreements.

traditions.name: Eastern Orthodoxy
traditions.summary: Eastern Orthodoxy is the communion of self-governing (autocephalous) churches rooted in the Greek-speaking Byzantine tradition, including the Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople and the Russian, Romanian, Serbian, Greek and other churches. It accepts the seven ecumenical councils and does not accept papal primacy of jurisdiction or the Western 'filioque' addition to the Nicene Creed. It understands itself as the continuation of the undivided church of the first millennium.

traditions.name: Catholic Church
traditions.summary: The Catholic Church is the communion of churches in full communion with the bishop of Rome, comprising the Latin Church and the Eastern Catholic churches. According to its teaching, it traces its origin to Jesus and the apostles, with Peter regarded as the first bishop of Rome, and it understands itself as the continuation of the undivided early church. The 1054 start date here marks only the conventional East–West division, not the church's own understanding of its founding.

sources.title: How Was the Catholic Church Founded?

traditions.name: Lutheranism
traditions.summary: Lutheranism is the branch of Protestantism that traces its theology to Martin Luther and the German Reformation, conventionally dated from the Ninety-five Theses of 31 October 1517. It teaches justification by grace through faith and the supreme authority of Scripture, with its doctrinal standards collected in the Book of Concord (1580). It is organised in autonomous regional and national churches, many linked through the Lutheran World Federation (1947).

traditions.name: Reformed & Presbyterian
traditions.summary: The Reformed tradition arose in the Swiss Reformation, beginning with Huldrych Zwingli's preaching in Zurich from 1519 and later shaped decisively by John Calvin in Geneva. It emphasises the sovereignty of God, the authority of Scripture and a simplified worship, and many of its churches adopted presbyterian government by elected elders. It spread to France, the Netherlands, Scotland (through John Knox), Hungary and North America.

traditions.name: Anglicanism
traditions.summary: Anglicanism originates in the Church of England, which separated from papal jurisdiction when Parliament passed the Act of Supremacy in 1534, declaring Henry VIII supreme head of the English church. Its identity was shaped by the Book of Common Prayer (1549; 1662) and the Thirty-nine Articles (1571), and it describes itself as both catholic and reformed. Today the churches of the Anglican Communion are loosely united around the Church of England and the Archbishop of Canterbury.

traditions.name: Anabaptists
traditions.summary: The Anabaptists were a 'radical' Reformation movement that taught that baptism should follow a personal confession of faith, and that the church should be a voluntary community of believers separate from state control. The Swiss Brethren formed near Zurich in January 1525, and the movement was widely persecuted by Catholic and Protestant authorities alike. Its living descendants include the Mennonites, Amish and Hutterites.

traditions.name: Baptists
traditions.summary: Baptists emerged from English Separatism when John Smyth's exiled congregation in Amsterdam adopted believer's baptism in 1609; Thomas Helwys led part of the group back to England, founding a church near London around 1611–12. Baptists teach baptism of professing believers (later typically by immersion), congregational autonomy and religious liberty. They became one of the largest Protestant families, especially in the United States.

traditions.name: Methodism
traditions.summary: Methodism grew out of the evangelical revival led by John and Charles Wesley within the Church of England, gaining momentum after John Wesley's Aldersgate experience of 24 May 1738. It emphasises personal assurance of salvation, holiness of life, disciplined small groups and lay preaching. American Methodists organised as a separate church at the Christmas Conference of 1784, and British Methodism separated formally from the Church of England in 1795.

traditions.name: Pentecostalism
traditions.summary: Pentecostalism is a renewal movement that teaches a post-conversion 'baptism in the Holy Spirit', often evidenced by speaking in tongues, together with divine healing and other spiritual gifts. It drew on the Wesleyan Holiness movement, Charles Fox Parham's teaching in Topeka (1901) and, above all, the Azusa Street revival in Los Angeles led by William J. Seymour from 1906. It has since become one of the fastest-growing forms of Christianity, especially in the Global South.

sources.title: Spirit and Power: A 10-Country Survey of Pentecostals (Preface)

traditions.name: Adventism
traditions.summary: Adventism grew out of the Millerite movement in the United States, which expected Christ's return in 1843–44 and experienced the 'Great Disappointment' of 22 October 1844. Several denominations emerged afterwards, the largest being the Seventh-day Adventist Church, formally organised in 1863, which teaches Saturday Sabbath observance and an imminent Second Coming. Ellen G. White, James White and Joseph Bates are regarded by the church as its co-founders.

traditions.name: Jehovah's Witnesses
traditions.summary: Jehovah's Witnesses developed from a Bible study group formed by Charles Taze Russell in Allegheny, Pennsylvania, in the early 1870s, whose magazine Zion's Watch Tower first appeared in July 1879. The movement, long known as the Bible Students, adopted the name Jehovah's Witnesses in 1931 under Joseph F. Rutherford. Witnesses teach that their beliefs are a restoration of first-century Christianity; they are known for door-to-door ministry and for rejecting the doctrine of the Trinity.

sources.title: Noteworthy Events in the Modern-day History of Jehovah's Witnesses

traditions.name: Latter Day Saints
traditions.summary: The Latter Day Saint movement began when Joseph Smith and associates organised the Church of Christ on 6 April 1830 in Fayette, New York, shortly after publishing the Book of Mormon. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, its largest body, describes itself as the restoration of the original church of Jesus Christ through modern prophets; historians such as Jan Shipps describe Mormonism as a new religious tradition. After Smith's death in 1844 the movement divided, producing bodies such as the Community of Christ.

sources.title: Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (LDS)
Our History
sources.publisher: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints

traditions.name: Islam
traditions.summary: Monotheistic tradition centred on the Qur'an, which Muslims believe was revealed to Muhammad starting c. 610 CE, according to Islamic tradition in a cave on Mount Hira near Mecca. Muslims regard Muhammad as the last in a line of prophets that includes Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses and Jesus. This entry represents the early, still-undivided community of believers around Muhammad, before later sectarian identities took shape.

traditions.name: Sunni Islam
traditions.summary: The majority branch of Islam. It accepts the first four caliphs, beginning with Abu Bakr, who was chosen as Muhammad's successor in 632, as legitimate leaders of the community. The 632 start date marks the succession dispute. Historians note that a distinct Sunni identity ('people of the sunna and the community') took shape gradually and only became fixed around the 9th–10th centuries.

sources.title: Adhering to the Community (Luzūm al-Jamāʿa): Continuities between Late Umayyad Political Discourse and 'Proto-Sunni' Identity (Abbas Barzegar)
sources.publisher: Review of Middle East Studies, Cambridge University Press

traditions.name: Shia Islam
traditions.summary: The second-largest branch of Islam. It holds that leadership of the community (the imamate) belonged to Ali ibn Abi Talib, Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law, and to his descendants through Fatima. Its roots lie in the 632 succession dispute. The killing of Ali's son Husayn at Karbala in 680 became a defining memory, and distinct Shia doctrines and branches (such as Twelver, Ismaili and Zaydi) developed over the following centuries.

traditions.name: Bábism
traditions.summary: Religious movement founded in Iran by Sayyid ʿAli Muhammad Shirazi, who took the title 'the Báb' ('the Gate') and declared his mission in Shiraz in May 1844. It emerged from a Twelver Shia background, especially the Shaykhi school. The authorities persecuted it heavily and executed the Báb in Tabriz in 1850. Ending it in 1863 is a modelling simplification: most Bábís went on to become Bahá'ís, but a small Azali Bábí minority, following Subh-i Azal, continued on its own.

traditions.name: Bahá'í Faith
traditions.summary: Religion founded by Mirza Husayn-ʿAli Nuri, known as Bahá'u'lláh. In April 1863, in the Garden of Ridván near Baghdad, he declared himself the figure foretold by the Báb. Bahá'ís understand their faith as an independent world religion that teaches the oneness of God, of religion and of humanity. Some scholars place it historically as an outgrowth of Bábism and, more distantly, of Shia Islam.

branches.reason: The Roman destruction of the Jerusalem Temple in 70 CE ended sacrificial worship and the priestly centre of Jewish life. According to the Talmudic account (whose historical accuracy scholars question), Yohanan ben Zakkai founded a centre of learning at Yavneh, and the sages, largely heirs of the Pharisaic tradition, rebuilt Judaism around Torah study, law and prayer.

Prayer and study in place of sacrifice
removed: Jerusalem Temple as sole cultic centre

sources.title: The Mishnah as a Response to Catastrophe

branches.reason: According to later Karaite and Rabbanite tradition, Anan ben David, passed over for the office of exilarch in the 760s, broke with the rabbinic academies and wrote a law code (c. 770) based on scripture rather than the Talmud. Modern scholars regard much of this story as later tradition: several non-rabbinic groups, including Anan's followers (Ananites), coalesced into Karaism from the mid-9th century, reaching institutional maturity in the 10th, and Anan was adopted retroactively as founder. Karaites themselves see their Judaism as the original form and the rabbinic Oral Torah as the innovation.
removed: Authority of the Talmud and rabbinic academies

branches.reason: In 18th-century Podolia a circle around the Ba'al Shem Tov, a healer and mystic, promoted a spirituality accessible to ordinary Jews, in a setting historians link to the aftermath of failed messianic movements and to an elite culture focused on Talmud study. After his death, disciples such as Dov Ber of Mezhirech spread it widely despite fierce opposition from the Mitnaggedim led by the Vilna Gaon; it remained within halakhic Judaism rather than rejecting it.

The tzaddik/rebbe as spiritual guide and intermediary

Scholarly framing: as Enlightenment, emancipation and the Reform movement challenged tradition in early 19th-century Central Europe, traditionalists organised a self-conscious defence of halakhah, led by figures such as Moses Sofer (Hatam Sofer) in Hungary and later Samson Raphael Hirsch in Frankfurt; the label 'Orthodox', at first often used by opponents, had acquired its religious meaning by the 1840s.

branches.reason: Influenced by the Enlightenment and the prospect of civic emancipation, the lay leader Israel Jacobson sought to make Jewish worship decorous and intelligible to modern Jews. On 17 July 1810 he dedicated a temple at his school in Seesen (Westphalia) with organ music, German hymns and prayers and a sermon, a milestone usually seen as the start of Reform; the first freestanding Reform temple followed in Hamburg in 1818.

branches.reason: Its intellectual roots lie with Zacharias Frankel, who walked out of the 1845 Frankfurt Reform rabbinical conference over the reduction of Hebrew in prayer and advocated 'positive-historical Judaism'. In America, reaction against the radical 1885 Pittsburgh Platform led traditionalists and moderate reformers (Sabato Morais and others) to found the Jewish Theological Seminary in New York in January 1886 (classes began in 1887); it was reorganised under Solomon Schechter in 1902. It is drawn here as a break from Reform, though it is also widely seen as a middle path between Reform and Orthodoxy.

branches.reason: The movement began among Jewish followers of Jesus of Nazareth, who after his crucifixion (sometime between c. 29 and 33 CE) proclaimed him the Messiah raised from the dead. Disputes over the messianic status of Jesus and whether Gentile converts must keep the Mosaic Law, together with the inclusion of Gentiles, gradually set the movement apart. Historians describe the 'parting of the ways' with Judaism as a gradual and regionally varied process stretching over several centuries rather than a single event.

Admission of Gentiles without full Torah observance

After the Council of Ephesus (431) condemned Nestorius, the church did not accept that council and aligned with the Antiochene (dyophysite) theology of Theodore of Mopsuestia. It calls itself the Church of the East; the Western label 'Nestorian' is regarded by the church as pejorative and by many scholars (e.g. Sebastian Brock) as a misleading misnomer.

branches.reason: The Council of Chalcedon (451) defined Christ as one person 'in two natures'. Many Christians in Egypt, Syria and Armenia judged this formula to be unfaithful to Cyril of Alexandria and too close to Nestorius, and held instead to 'one incarnate nature of the Word' (miaphysitism). Imperial attempts at reunion failed, and a separate hierarchy was firmly established by the sixth century; the WCC describes 451 as the first lasting ecclesial division.

Distinct Coptic, Syriac, Armenian and Ethiopian liturgical traditions

branches.reason: Long-standing linguistic, cultural and political estrangement between the Greek East and Latin West sharpened into disputes over papal authority, the Western addition of the 'filioque' to the Nicene Creed and practices such as leavened bread and clerical celibacy. In 1054 papal legates led by Cardinal Humbert and Patriarch Michael Cerularius of Constantinople exchanged excommunications, the conventional date of the schism. Historians stress that the split was a gradual process, hardened by the Crusades (notably the sack of Constantinople in 1204); the mutual excommunications were lifted in 1965, but full communion has not been restored.
removed: Universal jurisdiction of the bishop of Rome

branches.reason: The same East–West break of 1054 left the Latin Church in communion with the bishop of Rome, whose claims to primacy over all churches had been strongly asserted by the eleventh-century reform papacy. The Western church kept the filioque in the creed and continued its own liturgical and disciplinary practices. Like the Orthodox, the Catholic Church regards itself as the continuation of the undivided church rather than a new body; 1054 is only a conventional modelling date.

Martin Luther, an Augustinian friar and professor at Wittenberg, challenged the sale of indulgences in his Ninety-five Theses (31 October 1517), and his wider critique of church teaching led to his excommunication in 1521. German princes and cities adopted his reforms from the 1520s, and the Augsburg Confession (1530) gave the movement a doctrinal statement. Luther intended to reform the church, but the dispute ended in separate evangelical churches.

branches.reason: Huldrych Zwingli began preaching through the Gospels at Zurich's Grossmünster on 1 January 1519, and by 1523–25 the city had adopted his reforms, removing images and replacing the Mass with a simple communion service. Zwingli differed from Luther over the Lord's Supper, which he interpreted as a memorial. After Zwingli's death (1531), John Calvin in Geneva (from 1536/1541) shaped the tradition, which merged into a common Reformed confession (Second Helvetic Confession, 1560s).

branches.reason: When Pope Clement VII refused to annul Henry VIII's marriage to Catherine of Aragon, Parliament passed a series of acts cutting the English church's ties to Rome, culminating in the Act of Supremacy (1534), which declared the king supreme head of the Church of England. The initial break was primarily jurisdictional; Protestant doctrine and worship were introduced mainly under Edward VI and settled under Elizabeth I. Anglicans describe their church as both catholic and reformed.

After the Zurich council upheld infant baptism in January 1525, they performed the first adult (re)baptisms, probably on 21 January 1525, forming the Swiss Brethren. Authorities treated them as subversive, and many were imprisoned or executed.

branches.reason: English Separatists, who believed the Church of England was insufficiently reformed, formed independent congregations; John Smyth led one from Gainsborough into exile in Amsterdam in 1608. In 1609 Smyth concluded that only believers should be baptised, baptised himself and then others, forming what is usually regarded as the first Baptist church. Thomas Helwys returned with part of the group to England around 1611–12, where Baptist congregations developed into General and Particular Baptist streams.

Historians agree that such contacts existed but disagree about their extent: some (e.g. William Estep) argue for substantial Anabaptist influence on Baptist origins, while others stress the English Puritan-Separatist roots and see only limited influence or 'spiritual affinity'.

Wesley intended Methodism as a renewal movement within the Church of England, but his ordinations for America led to the Methodist Episcopal Church (1784), and British Methodists separated formally in 1795, after his death.

branches.reason: In April 1863, during a twelve-day stay in the Garden of Ridván near Baghdad, Bahá'u'lláh declared himself to his companions as the one foretold by the Báb. He made the claim public in Edirne around 1866, which led to a lasting split with his half-brother Subh-i Azal, whose followers (Azalis) stayed a minority. Bahá'ís see their faith as an independent world religion with its own revelation, not as a sect of Islam.
